interactions.label: A 55-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia is started on finasteride. S

params.question: A 55-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia is started on finasteride. Six months later his prostate has shrunk, but his muscle mass and strength remain unchanged. Which pharmacological property of finasteride best explains this selective outcome?

answers.text: Finasteride blocks the androgen receptor only in prostatic tissue

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Finasteride does not block the androgen receptor at all. It inhibits the enzyme 5-alpha reductase, which converts testosterone to DHT.

answers.text: Finasteride inhibits 5-alpha reductase, reducing DHT in the prostate while leaving testosterone's direct effects on muscle intact

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. DHT drives prostatic growth but muscle relies on testosterone itself, which is unaffected by finasteride. This tissue selectivity is why the prostate shrinks while muscle is spared.

answers.text: Finasteride selectively binds oestrogen receptors in muscle, preventing testosterone breakdown

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Finasteride has no action on oestrogen receptors. Its sole target is 5-alpha reductase, the enzyme that converts testosterone to DHT.

answers.text: Finasteride increases hepatic clearance of DHT without affecting circulating testosterone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Finasteride does not alter hepatic clearance. It blocks the conversion of testosterone to DHT at the tissue level by inhibiting 5-alpha reductase.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the distinction: DHT dominates in the prostate and scalp via tighter androgen receptor binding, while testosterone acts directly on muscle. Finasteride blocks 5-alpha reductase (the enzyme converting T → DHT), so prostatic DHT falls while muscle-bound testosterone is unaffected.

Well done. DHT binds the androgen receptor about five times more tightly than testosterone and dominates in the prostate and scalp, while testosterone acts directly on muscle and the hypothalamus — the basis for finasteride's selective clinical effect.

interactions.label: A 62-year-old man with erectile dysfunction is prescribed sildenafil 50 mg. Whic

params.question: A 62-year-old man with erectile dysfunction is prescribed sildenafil 50 mg. Which of the following drugs in his current medication list makes sildenafil absolutely contraindicated?

answers.text: Amlodipine 5 mg daily

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker used for hypertension. It does not act through the nitric oxide–cyclic GMP pathway and can be used alongside PDE5 inhibitors.

answers.text: Metformin 500 mg twice daily

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Metformin is an insulin sensitiser used in type 2 diabetes. It has no pharmacological interaction with PDE5 inhibitors.

answers.text: Isosorbide mononitrate 20 mg twice daily

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Isosorbide mononitrate is an organic nitrate. Nitrates release nitric oxide, raising cyclic GMP; sildenafil blocks cGMP breakdown. Together they cause dangerous, potentially fatal hypotension.

answers.text: Atorvastatin 40 mg daily

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Atorvastatin is a statin for hyperlipidaemia. It does not interact with the nitric oxide–cyclic GMP pathway and is safe with PDE5 inhibitors.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key rule: PDE5 inhibitors must never be combined with any nitrate. Both drugs raise cyclic GMP through the same pathway — nitrates by generating nitric oxide, PDE5 inhibitors by blocking cGMP breakdown — producing life-threatening hypotension.

Exactly right. Any nitrate — glyceryl trinitrate, isosorbide mononitrate, isosorbide dinitrate — is an absolute contraindication with PDE5 inhibitors because both amplify cyclic GMP–mediated vasodilation, risking severe hypotension.

interactions.label: A 30-year-old woman takes the progestogen-only pill (mini-pill) correctly every

params.question: A 30-year-old woman takes the progestogen-only pill (mini-pill) correctly every day. Despite this, she occasionally ovulates. Which mechanism continues to protect her from pregnancy in those cycles?

answers.text: Suppression of FSH prevents follicular development

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: FSH suppression is the primary mechanism of combined oral contraceptives, not the mini-pill. The fact that this woman is ovulating confirms that FSH suppression is not reliably occurring.

answers.text: Thickened cervical mucus blocks sperm transport

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Progestogen makes cervical mucus thick and impenetrable to sperm. This is the primary protective mechanism of the mini-pill and works even in cycles where ovulation is not suppressed.

answers.text: Accelerated tubal motility sweeps the ovum past the fertilisation window

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While progestogens can alter tubal motility, this is not the primary protective mechanism of the mini-pill. Cervical mucus thickening is the main barrier to sperm.

answers.text: Premature luteolysis shortens the luteal phase, preventing implantation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The mini-pill does not cause premature luteolysis. Its primary mechanism is thickening cervical mucus to block sperm, with endometrial thinning as a secondary backup.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the three targets: ovulation suppression (primary for COC/DMPA), cervical mucus thickening (primary for the mini-pill), and endometrial thinning (a backup). The mini-pill's main mechanism is making cervical mucus impenetrable to sperm.

Right. The progestogen-only pill relies primarily on cervical mucus thickening to block sperm. Even when ovulation breaks through, sperm cannot reach the ovum — a key difference from the combined pill's reliance on ovulation suppression.

interactions.label: A woman at 30 weeks of gestation presents with preterm contractions. Her obstetr

params.question: A woman at 30 weeks of gestation presents with preterm contractions. Her obstetrician decides to use a tocolytic drug. Based on the physiology of uterine contractility, which of the following is an appropriate drug mechanism to suppress her contractions?

answers.text: Stimulating oxytocin receptors to induce receptor desensitisation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Stimulating oxytocin receptors would trigger more contractions, not suppress them. Tocolytics work by blocking, not stimulating, the oxytocin receptor (e.g. atosiban).

answers.text: Blocking calcium entry into myometrial smooth muscle cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Calcium entry is essential for myometrial contraction. Calcium channel blockers like nifedipine prevent this, relaxing the uterus — one of the established tocolytic strategies.

answers.text: Increasing prostaglandin synthesis from the amnion and decidua

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Prostaglandins stimulate uterine contractions and ripen the cervix. Increasing their synthesis would worsen preterm labour, not suppress it.

answers.text: Promoting gap junction formation between myometrial cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Gap junctions allow contractions to synchronise across the myometrium. Promoting them would strengthen coordinated contractions — the opposite of what a tocolytic should achieve.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall the three tocolytic mechanisms: blocking the oxytocin receptor, blocking calcium entry into myometrial cells, or boosting cyclic AMP. Each reverses one of the pathways that switches the uterus from quiescence to active contraction.
Exactly. Tocolytics exploit the same pathways that drive labour — blocking oxytocin receptors, blocking calcium entry, or boosting cyclic AMP — to keep the uterus in its quiescent state.

interactions.label: In a woman with infertility caused by hyperprolactinaemia, how do dopamine agoni

params.question: In a woman with infertility caused by hyperprolactinaemia, how do dopamine agonists such as cabergoline restore ovulation?

answers.text: They directly stimulate follicular development in the ovary

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Dopamine agonists do not act on the ovary. They act on the anterior pituitary to lower prolactin, which indirectly restores the hormonal cascade needed for ovulation.

answers.text: They lower prolactin levels, removing the suppression of GnRH and thereby restoring FSH and LH secretion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Elevated prolactin suppresses GnRH pulsatility. By stimulating dopamine receptors on lactotrophs, cabergoline lowers prolactin, restoring normal GnRH, FSH, and LH secretion so ovulation can resume.

answers.text: They block oestrogen receptors in the hypothalamus, mimicking a low-oestrogen state that triggers FSH release

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes the mechanism of clomiphene, a selective oestrogen receptor modulator used for anovulation in PCOS — not the mechanism of dopamine agonists.

answers.text: They increase ovarian sensitivity to circulating gonadotropins

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Dopamine agonists do not alter ovarian sensitivity. They work upstream at the pituitary, lowering prolactin to relieve GnRH suppression and restore normal gonadotropin secretion.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the cause–drug logic: hyperprolactinaemia suppresses GnRH, which drops FSH and LH, blocking ovulation. Dopamine agonists (cabergoline, bromocriptine) lower prolactin at the pituitary, lifting that suppression and restoring the ovulatory cascade.
Well done. The chain is: dopamine agonist → lowers prolactin → removes GnRH suppression → restores FSH and LH → ovulation resumes. Each infertility cause maps to a specific pharmacological target.

interactions.label: A 65-year-old man with confirmed hypogonadism has a significantly enlarged prost

params.question: A 65-year-old man with confirmed hypogonadism has a significantly enlarged prostate causing moderate lower urinary tract symptoms and also reports erectile dysfunction. Which single drug can address both his urinary symptoms and erectile dysfunction simultaneously?

answers.text: Finasteride 5 mg daily

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Finasteride shrinks the prostate over 3–6 months by blocking DHT production, but it does not treat erectile dysfunction and may even worsen sexual function as an adverse effect.

answers.text: Tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Tamsulosin is an alpha-1 blocker that relaxes prostatic and bladder-neck smooth muscle, relieving urinary symptoms rapidly. However, it does not treat erectile dysfunction and can cause retrograde ejaculation.

answers.text: Tadalafil 5 mg daily

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Low-dose daily tadalafil relaxes smooth muscle in both the prostate and the corpus cavernosum through PDE5 inhibition, making it uniquely suited to treat both BPH/LUTS and ED concurrently.

answers.text: Sildenafil 50 mg on demand

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: On-demand sildenafil treats erectile dysfunction but is not indicated for BPH/LUTS. Tadalafil 5 mg daily is the PDE5 inhibitor with a dual indication for both conditions.

overallFeedback.feedback: When a patient has both BPH/LUTS and ED, tadalafil 5 mg daily covers both. Finasteride and tamsulosin address only the prostate, while on-demand sildenafil addresses only ED. Tadalafil's dual indication is a key prescribing advantage.

Exactly. Tadalafil 5 mg daily is the only PDE5 inhibitor approved for concurrent BPH/LUTS and ED management — its long half-life and smooth muscle relaxation in both the lower urinary tract and corpus cavernosum make it uniquely suited.
